function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends an HTTP GET request to retrieve Device Connector Versions information from a specified URL. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: The URL to which the GET request is sent. The URL points to a JSON file containing Device Connector Versions information.

params.description: Optional query parameters to include in the GET request as key-value pairs.

message.content:
Below is a quick‑reference guide for pulling *detailed* interface data from a network device. I’ll cover three common methods: | Method | Typical Use‑Case | Example Command / Call | |--------|------------------|------------------------| | **CLI** (text mode) | Quick manual check, troubleshooting, or scripting with expect/ssh | `show interface GigabitEthernet1/0/1` (Cisco)
`show interfaces terse | match ge-0/0/1` (Juniper) | | **RESTCONF / NETCONF** | Programmatic access, integration with SDN controllers, automation frameworks | `GET https:///restconf/data/Cisco-IOS-XE-native:native/interface/GigabitEthernet=1/0/1` | | **SNMP** | Monitoring, syslog aggregation, legacy systems | OID `.1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.1` (ifIndex), `.1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.8` (ifOperStatus) | --- ## 1. CLI – “show interface” ### Cisco IOS XE / IOS XR ```bash show interface GigabitEthernet1/0/1 ``` Typical output: ``` GigabitEthernet1/0/1 is up, line protocol is up Hardware is Gigabit Ethernet, address is 001b.7c5f.1234 (bia 001b.7c5f.1234) MTU 1500 bytes, BW 1000000 Kbit/sec, DLY 10 usec, Encapsulation ARPA, loopback not set Keepalive set (10 sec) Full-duplex, 1000Mb/s, media type is RJ45 ... Internet address is 192.168.1.1/24 Last input 00:00:12, last output 00:00:07, output hang never ... ``` ### Juniper JUNOS ```bash show interfaces terse | match ge-0/0/1 ``` Output snippet: ``` ge-0/0/1 up up 1000 1000 1000 1000 1000 1000 1000 1000 1000 1000 1000 1000 ``` For full detail: ```bash show interfaces ge-0/0/1 extensive ``` --- ## 2. RESTCONF (JSON) Assuming you have HTTPS + basic auth enabled on the device: ```http GET https:///restconf/data/Cisco-IOS-XE-native:native/interface/GigabitEthernet=1/0/1 Authorization: Basic Accept: application/yang-data+json ``` Sample JSON response (truncated): ```json { "Cisco-IOS-XE-native:interface": { "GigabitEthernet": [ { "name": "1/0/1", "description": "Uplink to Core", "ip": { "address": { "primary": { "addr": "192.168.1.1", "mask": "255.255.255.0" } } }, "status": "up", "line-protocol-status": "up", "speed": "1000", "duplex": "full", "mtu": 1500, "statistics": { "in-octets": 123456789, "out-octets": 987654321, "in-unicast-pkts": 12345, "out-unicast-pkts": 54321 } } ] } } ``` If you’re using NETCONF/YANG, the path would look similar but you’d send an XML `` RPC instead of a REST GET. --- ## 3. SNMP Using `snmpwalk` or a monitoring tool: ```bash snmpwalk -v2c -c public IF-MIB::ifTable ``` Key OIDs for interface status: | OID | Meaning | Example Value | |-----|---------|---------------| | `.1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.1` (`ifIndex`) | Interface index | `1` | | `.1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.2` (`ifDescr`) | Description | `GigabitEthernet1/0/1` | | `.1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.8` (`ifOperStatus`) | Operational status | `1` (up) | | `.1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.10` (`ifInOctets`) | Bytes received | `12345678` | | `.1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.16` (`ifOutOctets`) | Bytes transmitted | `87654321` | --- ## Putting It All Together | Scenario | Recommended Method | Why | |----------|--------------------|-----| | Manual troubleshooting | CLI | Fast, no extra tooling | | Automated inventory / configuration management | RESTCONF/NETCONF | Structured JSON/XML, easy to parse | | Long‑term monitoring / alerting | SNMP | Mature ecosystem, supported by most MIB browsers | Feel free to let me know which platform you’re working on (Cisco, Juniper, Arista, etc.) and I can tailor the exact command or API call for you!
